newsitem.title: SPAIN: Telefonica/P.Telecom deal portends wider alliance.
newsitem.headline: Telefonica/P.Telecom deal portends wider alliance.

text.p: Spain's Telefonica and Portugal Telecom teamed up in a share swap deal on Tuesday that analysts see as a prelude to a global alliance with Britain's BT and U.S.-based MCI.
News of the Iberian pennisula deal comes a day after the Portuguese operator announced it had chosen Concert, a BT/MCI alliance, as its partner in global telecommunications.
"It's starting to be clear that a four-part alliance is being formed, reinforced by share swaps among the various participants," said a foreign brokerage analyst in Madrid.

But Telefonica de Espana, which is seeking an American partner to give it access to the 40 million Spanish speakers in the United States, insists it is still in talks with AT&T, the largest U.S. operator, as well as BT/MCI.
BT said its shareholders approved the MCI alliance on Tuesday, and confirmed the Portugal Telecom deal, but refused to comment on Telefonica.
Industry analysts expect an announcement this week on what could mean a major reshuffling of European and American players on the telecommunications stage.

Telefonica is already aligned with AT&T through Unisource, a European group of Dutch, Swedish and Swiss operators. Most analysts believe it will break from that partnership, which lost money last year, and join up with AT&T's rival MCI.

Telefonica chairman Juan Villalonga is paying a visit to Portugal Telecom on Wednesday to iron out details of the share swap, which is expected to involve joint investment in Latin America, where they are already strong, and in North Africa.
Local media reports on Tuesday said Telefonica would get three percent of PT in exchange for one percent of Telefonica.
But the Iberian deal is really seen as a harbinger of four-part alliance of BT, MCI, Telefonica and Portugal Telecom.

"We wouldn't be surprised by such an alliance as we've always viewed Telefonica's participation in Unisource, which still hasn't had good results, with skepticism," a Madrid-based international portfolio manager said.
Portugal Telecom jumped the gun on Monday and announced by mistake that Telefonica had indeed signed up with BT/MCI, a bit of news that was immediately denied by all of the other parties.

Analysts said AT&T was probably making a big pitch to buy its way back into Telefonica's good graces, but most said the Spanish operator with its coveted position in the fast-growing Latin American markets would switch in the end to MCI.
"Its potential new partners seem much more attractive than Unisource, which just lost a bid for an important contract in France," the analyst said.
"Telefonica and PT control the Latin America market, while BT is the biggest operator in Europe which would compensate for the slightly more mediocre position of MCI with respect to its rival AT&T."

Telefonica has carefully built up a dominant position in Latin America over the past decade, buying up the state operators as they were privatised and investing at a time when the region's economies were far from stable.

It now calls itself the "undisputed leader in the Spanish-speaking world" with sales last year through its international subsidiary Telefonica Internacional-TISA of some 350 billion pesetas ($2.4 million).
The Spanish firm has major holdings in Peru, Chile, Argentina, Venezuela and Puerto Rico.
Telefonica also participated in a consortium that won 35 percent of the Brazilian operator Companhia Riograndense de Telecomunicacoes-CRT.
The deal with Portugal, which has a major part and an alliance with the main Brazilian operator Telebras, further seals Telefonica's position in the region.

"Telefonica first has to consolidate its Latin American participation, while the Asian market is much more difficult but with the help of BT and MCI it could give it new opportunities," another analyst said.
